summary.text: A 10-year-old boy presented with persistent left thigh pain that began three months prior and worsened over the past month, with a limp and a history of a fall from about 10 feet three months earlier. There was no associated fever, chronic steroid use, recent viral infection, blood dyscrasia or previous surgery. Symptomatic management at a local hospital failed and he was referred to an Orthopaedics outpatient department.

On presentation he had an antalgic gait on the left, an intact skin without increased temperature or tenderness, limited left hip motion and thigh circumference of 28 cm on the left versus 30 cm on the right. Plain radiographs and MRI showed over 25% epiphyseal involvement with flattening and findings consistent with osteonecrosis and secondary degenerative change of the left femoral head, classified as Catterall Type II and Herring Group B.

Because of financial limitations surgery was not undertaken. He was managed with analgesics and bilateral skin traction for three weeks, gradual abduction over 7 to 10 days and then a Petrie's cast, and was discharged with the cast and scheduled for monthly follow-ups with X-rays.

After four months of follow-up the round contour of the femoral head was regained, Petrie's cast was removed and the classification progressed to modified Stulberg I. He was advised to start non-weight-bearing physiotherapy and, after one week, to transition to weight-bearing activities, with gradual improvement over 6 months.
